classification.difficultyReason: Represent listed functions by their outputs and adapt diagonalisation by increasing each diagonal value while retaining natural-number outputs.

content.prompt: Consider the set of all functions of the form $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$. Using Cantor’s diagonalisation argument, show that this set is not countable.

answer.short:
The set is uncountable.

From any proposed list $f_1,f_2,\ldots$, construct $g(n)=f_n(n)+1$. Then $g$ differs from every listed function at its diagonal input.
answer.worked:
Suppose all functions $\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ can be listed as $f_1,f_2,f_3,\ldots$. Write $a_{ij}=f_i(j)$, so the list has the form
$$\begin{aligned}f_1&=(a_{11},a_{12},a_{13},\ldots),\\f_2&=(a_{21},a_{22},a_{23},\ldots),\\f_3&=(a_{31},a_{32},a_{33},\ldots),\\&\vdots\end{aligned}$$
Define $g:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ by $g(n)=a_{nn}+1$. Each output is a natural number. For every $n\in\mathbb N$,
$$g(n)=a_{nn}+1\ne a_{nn}=f_n(n).$$
Thus $g\ne f_n$ for every $n$, so $g$ is absent from the supposedly complete list. This is a contradiction. Therefore the set of all functions $\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ is uncountable.
